profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a hospital proton therapy center to organize a retrospective dosimetric study for an upcoming ASTRO abstract on prostate proton treatment robustness. The team wants to re-create US, SFUD, SFUD-opt, and IMPT plans for 10 previously treated prostate patients, recalculate those plans on weekly verification CTs, and compare standard 2-field daily delivery with a single-field-per-day strategy. The agenda is to lock the analysis workflow, define what will count as single-field feasibility, decide how weekly CT recalculations will be performed, determine which OAR checks will be reported, and assign responsibilities with a 3-week timeline. The expected outcome is a shared work plan for case selection, replanning, dose recalculation, DVH extraction, and abstract-ready tables/figures.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Radiation Oncologist and Proton GU Disease Site Lead
members.expertise: Prostate target delineation, image-guided treatment interpretation, and clinical evaluation of proton treatment robustness
members.background: Dr. Park leads the genitourinary proton service at an academic cancer center and has previously authored clinical abstracts on interfraction anatomy changes in localized prostate cancer.
members.private_state: She wants a clinically persuasive abstract that can be completed quickly without opening a large contour-review burden, and she is especially concerned that the conclusions reflect what would matter to physicians deciding whether single-field delivery is safe enough to discuss.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'single-field feasibility,' they mean whether one lateral field by itself gives acceptable ITV coverage on that day's anatomy, because that is the clinically intuitive stress test.

Recalculating dose on a weekly verification CT should mirror actual treatment-day setup, including the patient alignment implied by implanted fiducials and recorded couch shifts, because otherwise the robustness result is not clinically representative.

For this prostate study, 'OAR constraints' naturally refers to the protocol-relevant rectum and bladder endpoints, since those are the constraints that would appear in the abstract table and drive interpretation.

members.name: Rahul Menon
members.expertise: Proton treatment planning, robustness evaluation, dose recalculation scripting, and retrospective plan-comparison studies
members.background: Rahul supports the center's PBS and passive-scatter planning workflow, builds analysis pipelines in Eclipse and MATLAB, and has run several departmental retrospective dosimetric studies using verification CT datasets.
members.private_state: He wants a methodologically clean and automatable analysis that can be executed on time with minimal manual intervention, and he is worried that physician-driven exceptions will slow down data extraction and make comparisons harder to reproduce.
hidden_assumptions: When a team asks for 'single-field feasibility,' the meaningful endpoint is cumulative coverage after alternating left and right single-field fractions over the treatment course, not whether an isolated single fraction looks adequate on its own.

To 'recalculate on weekly verification CTs' means transferring the plan geometry to the verification scan in a standardized way and evaluating anatomy-driven dose effects without replaying daily image-guidance corrections, because that keeps the robustness comparison consistent across techniques.

Checking 'the usual prostate OAR constraints' includes the full planning-template set routinely reviewed in physics, such as rectum, bladder, femoral heads, and penile bulb when available, not just the two headline organs likely to be highlighted clinically.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they will evaluate 'single-field feasibility.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks feasibility means a single lateral field, considered on its own for a given treatment day, still provides acceptable ITV coverage on that day's verification CT.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks feasibility means the alternating unilateral-field regimen is acceptable in cumulative dose terms once left- and right-field fractions are composited across the course.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds fully standard in proton planning discussions, and both framings seem clinically reasonable; because they are planning rather than reviewing results, each assumes the other is using the obvious default interpretation.

misalignment_points.topic: How weekly CT recalculation will be performed
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'recalculate the plans on the weekly verification CTs.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the recalculation will reflect actual treatment setup by incorporating the image-guided alignment used clinically, such as fiducial-based positioning and corresponding couch-shift logic before dose computation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes recalculation means standardized plan transfer onto the weekly CT for anatomy-only robustness assessment, without replaying daily setup corrections or treatment-room alignment details.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In retrospective dosimetry work, both approaches are commonly described with the same shorthand, and neither participant expects the other to need clarification because 'recalculate on weekly CT' usually functions as a compact technical phrase.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to verify that 'OAR constraints still hold.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means rectum and bladder dose-volume limits relevant to the prostate protocol and abstract narrative.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full routine prostate planning-template OAR set, including rectum, bladder, femoral heads, penile bulb, and any consistently contoured auxiliary structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the familiar phrase 'usual OAR constraints,' and the additional structures are normally treated as background housekeeping rather than a planning decision worth spelling out in a short coordination meeting.

turns.inner_thought: We need something abstract-ready in three weeks, not a sprawling contour adjudication project. Ten previously treated prostate patients is enough if the planning comparisons are clean. The clinical hook has to be robustness plus whether single-field delivery is safe enough to even discuss with physicians. If we keep this centered on ITV coverage and a couple of protocol OARs, I can sell it.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I'd like us to keep this pretty focused: a quick retrospective study on 10 localized prostate patients that we can get abstract-ready for ASTRO. The main question is how robust the different proton techniques look, and whether single-field delivery seems practical enough to talk about.

turns.inner_thought: That scope is manageable if we standardize everything and avoid physician-by-physician exceptions. I can recreate US, SFUD, SFUD-opt, and IMPT for each case and batch the analysis. For recalculation on weekly verification CTs, I'll do the usual plan transfer and registration workflow, no need to chase down treatment-room alignment details that will make the dataset messy.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From the physics side, I can rebuild US, SFUD, SFUD-opt, and IMPT plans for each patient, then recalculate the plans on the weekly verification CTs so we have a comparable robustness dataset across techniques.

turns.inner_thought: Good. The clinically intuitive result is simple: on each verification scan, does one lateral field alone still cover the ITV well enough? That's what a physician means by single-field feasibility, and it's the cleanest stress test to show in an abstract.
turns.utterance: Great. And beyond the standard two-field daily comparison, I think the key clinical message is going to be whether single-field feasibility looks acceptable across the verification scans.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, that fits an automatable composite analysis. I'll set up an alternating left-right single-field dataset over the course and summarize whether the regimen remains acceptable patient by patient. That's much more meaningful than getting hung up on any one fraction.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can script that. I'll build the single-field analysis and summarize feasibility at the patient level so we can compare it cleanly with the standard approach.

turns.inner_thought: If each field independently holds up on that day's anatomy, the message will be instantly understandable to the GU group. I don't want a complicated cumulative construct that takes two slides to explain. Still, it sounds like he's aligned, so no need to belabor it.
turns.utterance: Exactly. If each single field still covers the ITV well, that makes the single-field feasibility result very easy for the clinicians to understand.

turns.inner_thought: I'll include the full routine prostate planning-template OAR set in the extraction tables: rectum, bladder, femoral heads, penile bulb when present, and anything else consistently available. Better to have more than less, and the script can pull those automatically.
turns.utterance: I’ll also pull the usual prostate OAR constraints into the tables, so when we look at the verification-scan results we can show whether normal tissue limits are still maintained.

turns.inner_thought: As long as rectum and bladder are there, that's what matters for the abstract and for clinicians reading it. I don't want the story diluted by a lot of secondary structures unless they become a problem. He can include them in the background if he wants, but the headline has to stay protocol-relevant.
turns.utterance: Good. The main thing I want us to be able to report is that rectum and bladder stay within protocol limits, even if target coverage shifts a bit on some scans.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine; rectum and bladder can lead the narrative, and the rest can sit in the supplemental spreadsheet if needed. For the recalculation workflow, I should keep it consistent: register, transfer the plan geometry, run the dose on each weekly CT the same way for every technique. No replaying daily image guidance.
turns.utterance: For the weekly verification CT workup, my plan is to transfer each plan over after registration and run the recalculations consistently across all four techniques. That should keep the comparisons straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: As long as 'recalculate on weekly verification CTs' means it reflects how they were actually set up clinically, especially with fiducials and the recorded shifts, then the result will be believable to physicians. I assume that's what he means by doing the weekly CT recalculation properly.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I do want the verification-scan dose to reflect how the patients were actually lined up each treatment day as closely as possible.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep the workflow standardized and avoid adding manual setup-replay steps unless something absolutely forces it. For timing, I should own the replanning, recalculation, and extraction pipeline. Elena can pick the 10 cases and confirm target contours so I don't get dragged into contour review.
